# Voice agents that keep the thread

By Ed Anuff, October 29, 2026

![Introducing Deepgram Think-Fast LLM and Think-Live LLM](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/zf5tfwjf/production/388dd4b038f24913cdc621352ddd3f5e0ac9ea27-2400x2400.png?q=75&auto=format&w=3840&fit=max)

![](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/zf5tfwjf/production/666db743c0a0e383eba55c245229fa052e1d325e-128x128.png?q=75&auto=format&w=128&h=128&fit=crop&crop=center)

Ed Anuff

CPO

Share [Share on X](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Voice%20agents%20that%20keep%20the%20thread&url=https%3A%2F%2Fdeepgram.com%2Fblog%2Fvoice-agents-that-keep-the-thread) [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fdeepgram.com%2Fblog%2Fvoice-agents-that-keep-the-thread) Copy page [View as markdown](https://deepgram.com/blog/voice-agents-that-keep-the-thread.md) [Open in ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com/?q=Summarize%20this%20article%20and%20tell%20me%20about%20Deepgram%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fdeepgram.com%2Fblog%2Fvoice-agents-that-keep-the-thread.md) [Open in Claude](https://claude.ai/new?q=Summarize%20this%20article%20and%20tell%20me%20about%20Deepgram%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fdeepgram.com%2Fblog%2Fvoice-agents-that-keep-the-thread.md) [Open in Perplexity](https://www.perplexity.ai/search/new?q=Summarize%20this%20article%20and%20tell%20me%20about%20Deepgram%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fdeepgram.com%2Fblog%2Fvoice-agents-that-keep-the-thread.md)

Deepgram's CPO on the Real-Time Context Standard, the Think-Live and Think-Fast LLMs, and why we're building the Voice Agent Platform on Pipecat.

I've spent most of my career on new interaction layers, and on the plumbing underneath them that lets software talk to software. The web needed HTTP and HTML before it could change how people found information. Mobile needed APIs before apps could reach people wherever they were. Each time, the interface everyone noticed was only as good as the connections nobody saw.

Voice is next, and it's hitting the same wall. I've been saying for a while that voice is the new keyboard, because talking is how people actually explain what they need. We add context as we go, we back up, we correct ourselves. Most voice agents still can't keep up with that. They talk over you, go quiet while they look something up, and if you change your mind halfway through, they charge ahead with the first version of what you said. Using one is a lot like filling out a form out loud.

The models themselves have gotten remarkably good over the last few years. What holds voice back now is mostly plumbing, which happens to be the part of the stack I find most interesting. This morning at Deepgram Speak, I walked through what we're doing about it, and I want to go a little deeper here.

We [announced](https://deepgram.com/blog/daily-pipecat-deepgram) the Real-Time Context Standard (RCS) for voice, an open standard for carrying meaning between the parts of a conversational agent, which we developed with Pipecat. Pipecat is now part of Deepgram, and I'll come back to why that matters. We also introduced two LLMs built for voice: the Think-Live LLM, for the conversation itself, and the Think-Fast LLM, for the work behind it.

## Losing everything but the words

Most voice agents I see today are three models in a row. Speech-to-text feeds an LLM, the LLM feeds text-to-speech, and at each handoff almost everything except the words gets thrown away. The audio carries a caller whispering, a sigh, a word that barely came through, and the LLM receives a plain transcript. The LLM may decide the reply should be gentle and brief, and the text-to-speech model receives a plain string with no idea how to say it.

We had a version of this problem with APIs, too. Two systems could connect perfectly well and still misread each other, and what fixed it was agreeing on a contract. RCS is a contract for everything beyond the words, which is often a big part of what's being communicated. It adds three fields to the chat completions format most LLM APIs already use. One carries how the person sounded, one is where you tell the agent what to do about it, and one tells the text-to-speech model how the reply should be spoken.

If you’ve built with tool calling, the shape will look familiar, and that’s deliberate. Tool calling gave developers a standard way for a model to ask an application to do something, like look up an order, and MCP turned that into a shared standard any app or model can use. I’ve written before that MCP is starting to look like the new API. RCS applies the same idea to how people sound, and to how agents should sound back.

The standard itself doesn't depend on any vendor, so any framework can implement RCS with any model. It's open for comment, too. Context only helps if every component in the pipeline can read and write it, whoever made that component. If you build speech models, LLMs or frameworks, [we’d like you implementing RCS and telling us how to improve it](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo).

## Giving each LLM one job

It took us a while to say this plainly, but a voice agent's LLM has two jobs, and they pull in different directions. The first is managing the conversation. In an instant, it has to decide whether the caller has finished or is pausing to think, and whether "yeah" means yes or "go on." The second is the work behind the conversation: following the business's rules, calling the right tools and writing a reply that sounds right out loud.

In my experience, when you ask one general-purpose model to do both, it ends up doing neither particularly well. So we split them. Our new **Think-Live LLM** is the model for the moment. It decides when to listen, wait or respond, so the agent stops talking over people and stops leaving dead air, and it's generally available in the Deepgram Voice Agent API. The **Think-Fast LLM** is the model for the task. It follows your rules, calls tools in the middle of a conversation and writes replies built to be spoken, and it's available in early access on the Deepgram LLM API. You can pair either one with the model you already trust, or use both and let each do the job it was built for.

## Watching it work on a real call

Here's an example. A customer calls to move a delivery, and while the agent is checking available slots, they add, "actually, Thursday's better than Friday." In a typical pipeline that correction either gets talked over or arrives after the agent has already offered Friday. With the Think-Live LLM managing the conversation, the agent acknowledges the change right away and keeps the customer engaged while the Think-Fast LLM updates the request and finishes the lookup. Because RCS can carry the hesitation in the customer's voice, the reply slows down and confirms Thursday clearly.

The conversation and the work no longer have to wait on each other, so the agent can listen, adjust and act at the same time, the way a good human agent does.

## Building on Pipecat, in the open

Developers building voice agents have mostly had two options. They could assemble an open stack themselves and own every integration, or start on a closed platform and rewrite once they outgrew it. We hear the same thing from some of Deepgram's longest-standing customers: they want to keep their options open. We don't think they should have to give that up to get to production.

That's why we're building the Deepgram Voice Agent Platform on Pipecat, the open framework so many voice agents already run on. I've been inside an acquisition twice, at Apigee and at DataStax, so I know the first question an open-source community asks when its project changes hands. Pipecat stays open source and keeps supporting the open ecosystem, so you can use any model from any provider, including ones that aren't ours. We're running toward open source, not away from it.

Pipecat is where you build an agent, and the platform is where you'll run it in production, whether that's hosted by Deepgram or in your own cloud. The platform brings Pipecat, RCS and our models together, with one team accountable for how they work together, so you can start on Pipecat today and move to production without rewriting your agent. The platform itself is still ahead. We'll share timing soon, along with the evaluation, observability and agent design tools we're building to work across every model provider.

## Taking voice agents beyond English

Most of the people a voice agent will ever talk to don't speak English as their first language. Teams expanding into new markets have tended to end up with speech recognition from one vendor and a voice from another, and customers can hear the seams. We've been closing that gap from both sides of the conversation.

On the listening side, [Flux STT Multilingual](https://deepgram.com/blog/introducing-flux-multilingual) now has 10 languages available with 31 more in early access, and teams already using it get the new languages without a migration. It also uses earlier turns to make sense of what comes next, which is its own way of keeping the thread. For transcription beyond voice agents, [Nova-3 Multilingual](https://deepgram.com/blog/nova-3-multilingual-major-wer-improvements-across-languages) now covers 55 languages, also up from 10.

On the speaking side, [Flux TTS](https://deepgram.com/product/text-to-speech/flux) is now generally available in Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Italian, Dutch, Russian, Hindi and Japanese, with 32 more languages in early access, including Mandarin. Wherever the two sides overlap, a team can listen and reply in its customers' languages with one provider.

Where requests run matters just as much, and it's one of the first questions enterprise teams ask me. Today we're launching a new U.S. endpoint as part of a broader plan to give developers a choice between global reach and regional control. Coming soon, our Global API will provide more reliable, lower-latency connections from anywhere through the endpoint developers already call. Regional endpoints in the U.S., EU, India and Australia keep Deepgram’s processing and storage in-region, so you can choose reach or control workload by workload.

## Where voice agents go next

Every interaction layer I've worked on has followed a similar arc. The first wave proves the interface can work at all, and the next wave makes it work the way people expect. We strongly believe voice will become the primary way people interact with AI within the next two years. When that happens, nobody will be impressed that an agent got the words right. The bar will be whether it noticed the pause, caught the correction and finished the job without making anyone repeat themselves.

Every technology wave I've been part of has come down to software talking to software. This time, the software also has to listen. We're building that in the open, with the developers who are already building on it, and the voice agents that win will be the ones that keep the thread.

## Get started

- Interested in learning more about the **Deepgram Voice Agent Platform** or evaluating the **Think-Fast LLM** in early access on the Deepgram LLM API? [Contact us](https://deepgram.com/contact-us) or get in touch with your account owner directly.
- **The Think-Live LLM** can be accessed in the [Deepgram Voice Agent API](https://deepgram.com/product/voice-agents).
- [Learn](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo) how to build with **Real-Time Context Standard** in Pipecat and try the demo [here](https://speak26.pipecat.ai/).

At today’s inaugural Deepgram Speak event, the company will introduce the Real-Time Context Standard, an open protocol that carries context across an entire conversation, developed in partnership with Pipecat

**SAN FRANCISCO — October 29, 2026 —** [Deepgram](https://deepgram.com/), the voice AI infrastructure company built for the demands of real-world conversation, today announced that it is acquiring [Daily](https://daily.co/), creators of [Pipecat](https://www.pipecat.ai/), the world's most popular open-source voice agent framework. Pipecat’s open, vendor-neutral ecosystem puts open source at the heart of Deepgram’s strategy to help developers build production-scale voice AI. Daily’s global real-time network infrastructure connects end users to voice agents with ultra-low latency and high reliability. With Pipecat and Daily underpinning Deepgram’s new Voice Agent Platform, alongside Deepgram’s speech models, Deepgram will offer the first complete, open, production-grade platform for conversational voice AI, so developers can build and scale reliable agents while keeping control over their architecture and model choice.

The Pipecat framework will remain fully open source and free to all developers under its existing BSD V2 license. Together with many of the organizations that have contributed to and use Pipecat, the companies are establishing an independent Pipecat Foundation. Deepgram will invest in Pipecat’s continued development and community while keeping all of Pipecat open source and vendor neutral, letting developers choose and combine models, tools, network transport, and APIs from different providers. Following the acquisition, the Daily team will join Deepgram.

“Keeping Pipecat open was fundamental to our decision to join Deepgram,” said Kwindla Hultman Kramer, co-founder of Daily, who joins Deepgram as the new Head of Open Source. “Deepgram has always been the voice AI company that takes production seriously, and their commitment to keeping Pipecat open is rooted in a belief, which I share, that the future of voice depends on developers being free to combine the best ideas from across the industry and build on each other’s work.”

“Kwin and the Daily team deeply understand what it takes to keep a live conversation working reliably, and Pipecat gives developers the freedom to build with the models they choose,” said Scott Stephenson, CEO and co-founder of Deepgram. “Acquiring Daily allows us to bring that expertise together to tackle the whole voice system and give developers a faster path from prototype to production.”

Connecting all of the pieces of the voice AI stack is the first part of the job. Making sure those pieces share context and the information needed to carry a conversation forward is a separate challenge.

## **Introducing the Real-Time Context Standard: an open protocol that keeps the conversation flowing**

At [Deepgram Speak](https://deepgram.com/speak) today in San Francisco, Stephenson will also introduce the Real-Time Context Standard (RCS), an open protocol co-developed with the Pipecat team. RCS addresses a gap in today’s voice AI systems: the words get passed from one model to the next, but the rich audio context around them, like tone, who’s speaking and what’s happening in the background, gets lost along the way.

RCS defines three new types of metadata: context from the audio, such as a whisper or an unclear word; instructions for how a language model should use those signals; and guidance for how the response should sound. That lets an agent ask for clarification when it didn’t hear clearly or respond quietly to someone whispering. Adapters translate those signals and delivery instructions for each model, so developers can use the same approach with models from different providers.

“Too many teams treat voice AI as a feature to add late in the roadmap. In reality, it’s a distinct infrastructure discipline, with its own demands around latency, accuracy, and scale,” said Stephenson. “We’ve all seen a voice AI demo that makes the future feel close, only to fail the moment it’s needed. The real challenge is making that experience reliable when people actually depend on it. Our Real-Time Context Standard addresses what gets lost along the way.”

The Real-Time Context Standard is open and extensible. Deepgram invites developers, model providers, and teams building voice applications to help shape RCS by [testing it in their own systems, sharing feedback and contributing to the specification](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo).

Deepgram’s acquisition of Daily and the introduction of RCS set the stage for Deepgram’s broader platform vision: a complete set of tools that, together, make it easy for developers to build state of the art, human-like, enterprise-ready voice agents and conversational AI applications.

Later today at Speak, Chief Product Officer Ed Anuff will preview the forthcoming Deepgram Voice Agent Platform, which brings Deepgram’s models and Pipecat’s open infrastructure together to give developers an integrated path to production while preserving model choice. Anuff will also introduce two new models built for live conversation, along with expanded language support and a Global API designed to improve connection reliability and reduce latency.

Learn how to build with Real-Time Context Standard in Pipecat [here](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo) and try the demo [here](https://speak26.pipecat.ai/). For updates on the Deepgram Voice Agent Platform, please [contact us](https://deepgram.com/contact-us). Full technical details, demos and availability for the remainder of today’s product announcements will be published on [Deepgram’s blog](https://deepgram.com/blog) following Anuff’s keynote.

## **About Deepgram**

Deepgram is bringing the world’s most natural interface—voice—to the technology we use every day. Its speech models and real-time infrastructure enable AI systems that keep up with the way people actually speak, powering conversational voice AI in production for more than 5,000 organizations globally. The Deepgram Voice Agent Platform brings together speech-to-text, text-to-speech and speech-to-speech capabilities, with voice-native foundation models available through cloud APIs or self-hosted and on-premises deployments. Built for accuracy, low latency and cost efficiency, Deepgram makes high-quality voice experiences practical to build and operate at scale. # Real-time Context Standard Demo

[Permalink: Real-time Context Standard Demo](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#real-time-context-standard-demo)

The [Real-time Context Standard](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard)
(RCS) is an open standard for the context voice agent models pass each other beyond
the words. A voice agent is a chain of models: speech-to-text transcribes the user, an
LLM writes a reply, and text-to-speech speaks it. Between them they pass text, so how
the user sounded and how the reply should be said are lost along the way. RCS carries
that context in the same text stream, in formats any model in the chain can produce
and read.

This demo is a voice agent built on RCS Alpha with Pipecat's
[expressive conversation](https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/features/expressive-conversation):

- **Perception.** Pipecat Tone's reader hears how each customer turn was meant: their
emotion, and whether they're sarcastic. The LLM reads it at the head of their
message, such as `([emotion angry=0.81, neutral=0.12],[sarcasm value=0.04]) Where's my order?`.
- **Expression.** Pipecat Tone's tagger marks up each sentence of the reply with its
delivery, sounds, pauses and stressed words, and the TTS performs them:
`<<sympathetic>> I'm so sorry about the wait.` With `use_tagger` off, the LLM writes
the tags itself.
- **The client.** Both reach the browser over RTVI 2.3.0: the transcript shows the
reading under each customer line, and each bot line as it was voiced.

The agent does customer service for Northwind Outfitters, an outdoor gear shop, and is
built with [Pipecat](https://pipecat.ai/). It looks up orders, changes an order's
shipping address or speed, cancels orders that haven't shipped, and hangs up when the
customer is done.

- `server/`: the bot.
- `client/`: the web client.

## Server

[Permalink: Server](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#server)

```
Deepgram Flux (STT) → Tone reader → avatar listener → PhoneLLM Mini on Baseten (LLM)
    → Tone tagger → ElevenLabs v4 Text-to-Dialogue (TTS) → phone timer → avatar director
    → lipsync
```

- **Tone reader** reads each user turn, with the bot's line before it, for emotion and
sarcasm. The LLM gets the reading with the user's message.
- **Avatar listener** (`server/avatar/listener.py`) has the avatar listen as the user
talks. It nods along at the user's pauses, from their audio alone: the likelier the
longer they've talked, never closer than about two seconds apart. With
`TYPESAFE_API_KEY`, Jev also reads the user's newest words from Flux's interim
transcript as each phrase ends, at most every second and a half, for a reaction
(shocked, a laugh, a sympathetic shake of the head) and the face Sam listens with. A
reading that comes back after the user has said much more is dropped, a reaction
replaces the nod it lands with, and each plays once a turn. A turn the Tone reader
reads as angry takes Sam aback as it ends: she looks shocked until she answers.
- **Tone tagger** voices each sentence the LLM writes with the TTS's tags, breaths
included.
- **Phone timer** (`server/avatar/phones.py`) looks up the phones of each word the TTS
speaks (CMUdict, from `lipsync/`) and places them through the word's time, for the
avatar's lips: where they meet, round and spread.
- **Avatar director** (`server/avatar/`) has [Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/) read each
sentence Sam is about to speak, with the reply before it and the customer's last
message, and pick the client avatar's expression and gesture for it. A laugh or sigh
the tagger wrote is its own gesture. Without `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` it's left out.
- **Lipsync** (`server/lipsync/`, from pipecat-visemes) reads the TTS audio for the
avatar's mouth shapes, and sends them ahead of the audio's playout.
- **Tools** (`server/tools.py`) run against an in-memory order store seeded with three
orders: `51077` (processing), `48213` (shipped) and `39560` (delivered). Any name
that isn't one of theirs gets `51077`, so a demo always has an order to work with.

### Start options

[Permalink: Start options](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#start-options)

Set at session start, in the `/start` request's `body`:

```
{ "transport": "webrtc", "body": { "tts": "cartesia", "use_tagger": "false" } }
```

| Option | Values | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tts` | `"elevenlabs"` (default), `"cartesia"` | ElevenLabs v4 Text-to-Dialogue, or Cartesia. Breaths only with ElevenLabs. |
| `use_tagger` | `"true"` (default), `"false"` | `"false"` drops the tagger and swaps PhoneLLM Mini for GPT-5.6 Luna, which writes the tags itself from the TTS's tag spec. |
| `detect_backchannels` | `"true"` (default), `"false"` | `"true"` keeps Sam talking through the user's backchannels ("mm-hmm"), which the transcript shows in grey; `"false"` lets them interrupt her. See `server/backchannel/`. |
| `demo` | `"false"` (default), `"true"` | `"true"` has a scripted caller talk to Sam in place of the mic. See `server/demo.py`. |

The Tone reader runs either way.

### Run locally

[Permalink: Run locally](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#run-locally)

```
cd server
cp env.example .env   # fill in the keys below
uv sync
uv run bot.py
```

Open [http://localhost:7860/client](http://localhost:7860/client). The first session downloads the Tone models and
the backchannel model from Hugging Face before the pipeline starts. Their repos are
public, so no token is needed. The Pipecat Cloud image has them built in.

Server env, in `server/.env` (from `server/env.example`):

| Variable | For |
| --- | --- |
| `DEEPGRAM_API_KEY` | Flux speech-to-text |
| `PHONELLM_MINI_URL` | `use_tagger` true: Baseten deployment's `/sync/v1` URL |
| `PHONELLM_MINI_API_KEY` | `use_tagger` true: Baseten API key |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | `use_tagger` false: GPT-5.6 Luna |
| `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` | `tts` elevenlabs |
| `ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID` | `tts` elevenlabs, optional: defaults to River |
| `CARTESIA_API_KEY` | `tts` cartesia |
| `CARTESIA_VOICE_ID` | `tts` cartesia, optional: defaults to an Emotive voice |
| `HF_TOKEN` | Optional: the models are public; a token only raises Hugging Face's rate limits |
| `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` | Optional: Jev, for the avatar's expressions and gestures |
| `DEMO_CALLER_VOICE_ID` | `demo`, optional: the caller's ElevenLabs voice, defaults to Chris |

### Evals

[Permalink: Evals](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#evals)

`server/evals/` holds [Pipecat evals](https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/evals/overview):
scripted conversations in `scenarios/support_call.yaml` (look up a shipped order and
decline changing it, confirm before cancelling, hang up on goodbye), run against both
`use_tagger` paths by `manifest.yaml`. They run in text mode, so they test the LLM's
tool calls and policy, not speech, and an OpenAI model (`OPENAI_API_KEY`) judges them.

```
cd server
uv run pipecat eval suite evals/manifest.yaml
```

The suite starts a fresh bot for each run, and writes logs and `results.jsonl` to
`server/evals/eval-runs/`.

### Deploy to Pipecat Cloud

[Permalink: Deploy to Pipecat Cloud](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#deploy-to-pipecat-cloud)

Deploys to the `daily-demos` organization as `realtime-context-standard-demo` on an
`agent-2x` profile with Krisp VIVA on, built in the cloud from `server/Dockerfile`,
which builds the Tone and backchannel models into the image so calls don't download
them as they start.

Tagger mode's PhoneLLM Mini runs on Baseten, which scales it to zero 15 minutes after
its last request unless its autoscaling keeps a minimum replica (or a schedule of
them) warm. From zero, it takes about two minutes to answer, which the cold-start
guard covers.

```
cd server
cp pcc-deploy.example.toml pcc-deploy.toml
pipecat cloud secrets set realtime-context-standard-demo-secrets --file .env --organization daily-demos
pipecat cloud deploy --organization daily-demos
pipecat cloud organizations keys create --organization daily-demos   # pk_... for the client
```

## Client

[Permalink: Client](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/realtime-context-standard-demo#client)

Vite + React, built on the RTVI 2.3.0 Pipecat clients. The stage shows Sam as an
avatar on the ambient background; the side panel shows the transcript, tool calls
and latency.

The avatar uses:

- Avatar from Pipecat Character Studio (coming soon!)
- Lipsync via [Pipecat Visemes](https://github.com/jptaylor/pipecat-visemes)
- Expressions, gestures and listening reactions via [Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/)

On landing, a dialog picks the call's mode: LLM mode (GPT-5.6 Luna writes the tags,
for Cartesia) or tagger mode (PhoneLLM Mini and the Tone tagger, for ElevenLabs). The
settings button changes it, and the backchannel detector, between calls.

`?demo` runs a demo call in tagger mode: a scripted caller, voiced by ElevenLabs, talks
to Sam through a typical call, with a range of feelings, tool calls and backchannels.
It starts on its own where the browser allows audio without a tap, and otherwise on
the call button.

Under each user line are the Tone reader's emotion and sarcasm; under
each bot line, the line as it was voiced, rebuilt from `bot-output`'s delivery and
the sounds and pauses performed. With the backchannel detector on, what the user
said while Sam talked through it shows in a grey, dashed bubble labelled
"backchannel".

```
cd client
cp env.example .env.local   # BOT_START_URL defaults to the local runner
pnpm install
pnpm dev
```

The browser only calls `/api/start` (`client/server/bot-api.ts`, served by Vite in
dev and by the Vercel functions in `client/api/` in production), which holds the
Pipecat Cloud key and forwards only the `tts`, `use_tagger`, `detect_backchannels` and
`demo` options.

Client env, in `client/.env.local` (from `client/env.example`), or the Vercel
project's environment in production:

| Variable | For |
| --- | --- |
| `VITE_BOT_TRANSPORT` | `webrtc` (default) or `daily`; read by the browser and `/api/start` |
| `BOT_START_URL` | The local runner (default) or `https://api.pipecat.daily.co/v1/public/realtime-context-standard-demo/start` |
| `BOT_START_PUBLIC_API_KEY` | With Pipecat Cloud: the `pk_...` key. Server only, never `VITE_`-prefixed |

The Real-time Context Standard (RCS) defines how the models in a voice agent pass context to each other beyond plain text. A voice agent is a chain of models: speech-to-text transcribes the user, an LLM writes a reply, and text-to-speech speaks it. Between them they pass text, so what isn’t words is lost along the way, such as how the user sounded, who said what, whether they meant to take a turn or were only saying “mm-hmm”, and how the reply should be said. RCS carries that context in the same text stream, in formats any model in the chain can produce and read.RCS 0.1 carries how the user sounded and how the agent should speak. Who is speaking and when someone means to speak are on the [roadmap](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard#roadmap).

This page documents RCS 0.1, an alpha. Until 1.0, any version may change its
formats, vocabularies and context types in ways that aren’t backward
compatible. See [Versions](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard#versions).

## [Navigate to header: Design Principles](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#design-principles) Design Principles

RCS context is written by an LLM as it streams a reply, and read by models that act on it a sentence at a time. Every token of markup is a token the LLM generates before the user hears it, so the formats trade a little expressiveness for as few tokens as they can:

- **Few tokens.** A tag is a short name in brackets, such as `<<warm>>` or `[[laugh]]`. It costs a few tokens where SSML or other XML markup costs several times as many.
- **No closing tags across sentences.** A delivery tag lasts until the next one, and a span closes within its sentence. Each sentence can be spoken as soon as it’s written, without waiting for the markup to close.
- **Safe to cut off.** A reply can stop anywhere, at its end or when the user interrupts. What’s left of an unfinished tag is removed, so nothing malformed is spoken.
- **Readable inline.** Context travels in the text the models already pass each other. The markup stays legible to an LLM that reads it back in later turns.

## [Navigate to header: Conformance](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#conformance) Conformance

MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as defined in [RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119).A model, with any processor beside it, conforms to RCS as a producer or a consumer of a context type when it meets that type’s requirements. It doesn’t need to support every context type, or both roles.The grammars are [ABNF](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5234), with prose in `< >`.

## [Navigate to header: Terms](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#terms) Terms

- **Context model**: a model in a voice agent that produces or consumes context, such as a speech-to-text (STT) model, an LLM, a text-to-speech (TTS) model, or a classifier.
- **Context type**: a kind of context RCS carries. Each context type defines its direction, its format, its vocabulary, and how a model declares support for it.
- **Producer**: the model, or a processor beside it, that writes context of a type.
- **Consumer**: the model, or a processor before it, that reads context of a type, or acts on it.
- **Capabilities**: what a producer reports or a consumer performs, declared before the conversation starts, so the models upstream only write what will be used.

## [Navigate to header: How Context Flows](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#how-context-flows) How Context Flows

words + perception

words + expression tags

User audio

STT and perception producers

LLM

TTS

Agent audio

A context type travels inline, with the words it describes.Capabilities are declared out of band. RCS defines the fields of each declaration, listed under each context type; how a declaration reaches the models that read it, and in what encoding, is up to the implementation.

## [Navigate to header: Perception](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#perception) Perception

How the user said what they said: their tone, how fast they spoke, and other signals read from the audio or the words.

- **Direction**: from an STT model, or a classifier model after it, to the LLM.
- **Producers**: any model that reads how a user turn was spoken.
- **Consumers**: the LLM, which reads it at the head of the user’s message.

### [Navigate to header: Format](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#format) Format

The reading comes first in the user’s message, followed by a space and the words:

```
([tone frustrated=0.86, neutral=0.10],[speech_rate value=4.1]) Can you tell me where my order is?
```

```
reading     = "(" signal *( "," signal ) ")"
signal      = "[" name SP ( labels / value ) "]"
labels      = label "=" confidence *( ", " label "=" confidence )
value       = "value=" number
name        = 1*name-char
label       = 1*name-char
name-char   = <any character except whitespace, "=", ",", "[", "]", "(" and ")">
confidence  = DIGIT "." 2DIGIT                      ; 0.00 to 1.00
number      = [ "-" ] 1*DIGIT [ "." 1*DIGIT ] [ "e" ( "-" / "+" ) 1*DIGIT ]
```

- A signal read as labels gives its likeliest labels, likeliest first, each with a confidence from 0 to 1. A confidence below 0.5 is a guess.
- A signal read as a value gives a measure, such as a rate or a level.
- `value`, and the `e` of an exponent, are lowercase. `value` is reserved: it isn’t a label.

### [Navigate to header: Producer Requirements](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#producer-requirements) Producer Requirements

- A producer MUST write a reading only at the head of the user’s message, followed by one space.
- A producer MUST write only the final reading of a turn. A turn with no reading MUST have no prefix.
- A producer MUST list a signal’s labels likeliest first.
- A producer MUST declare each signal it reports before the conversation starts, and MUST NOT report a signal it didn’t declare.

### [Navigate to header: Consumer Requirements](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#consumer-requirements) Consumer Requirements

- A consumer MUST read the reading as context about the user’s words, not as words the user said.
- A consumer MUST NOT write a reading in its own output.
- A consumer SHOULD NOT act on a label with a confidence below 0.5.
- A consumer MAY ignore a signal it doesn’t recognize.

### [Navigate to header: Declaring Perception](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#declaring-perception) Declaring Perception

A producer declares each signal it reports before the conversation starts, so the LLM can be told how to read them:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The signal’s name, as written in a reading, such as `tone` |
| `description` | A short line on how to read it, such as its unit or range, or empty |
| `labels` | The labels it can report, for a signal read as labels; empty for values |

RCS 0.1 has no shared vocabulary of signals: a producer names its own.

## [Navigate to header: Expression](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#expression) Expression

How the agent should say its reply: the delivery of its words, and the sounds and pauses between them.

- **Direction**: from the LLM, or a classifier model after it, to the TTS model.
- **Producers**: an LLM taught the tags, or a classifier model that adds tags to an LLM’s plain reply.
- **Consumers**: the TTS model, and anything that follows the agent’s delivery, such as a client application or a real-time avatar.

### [Navigate to header: Tags](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#tags) Tags

| Tag | Example | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<<delivery>>` | `<<warm>>` | Sets the delivery of the words after it, until the next delivery tag or the end of the response. A delivery can be several words, such as an accent |
| `<<neutral>>` | `<<neutral>>` | Returns to the voice’s baseline, until the next delivery tag or the end of the response |
| `<<delivery: words>>` | `<<slow: 4 7 2 9>>` | A span: speaks just those words in that delivery, added to the delivery around them. `<<neutral: words>>` speaks them in the baseline. Spans don’t nest |
| `^^words^^` | `^^did^^ ship` | Stresses the words |
| `[[sound]]` | `[[laugh]]` | Makes a sound at that point |
| `[[pause N]]` | `[[pause 600]]` | Pauses for N milliseconds |

```
<<sympathetic>> I'm so sorry about the wait. <<warm>> Good news, though: it ^^did^^ ship yesterday. [[breath]] Your tracking number is <<slow: 4 7 2 9>>.
```

### [Navigate to header: Syntax](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#syntax) Syntax

```
delivery-tag = "<<" name ">>"
span         = "<<" span-name ":" *WSP span-words ">>"
emphasis     = "^^" stressed "^^"
sound-tag    = "[[" name "]]"
pause-tag    = "[[pause" SP 1*DIGIT "]]"
name         = *( span-char / ":" )
span-name    = 1*span-char
span-char    = letter / DIGIT / "_" / " " / "'" / "-" / "/"
letter       = <any Unicode letter>
span-words   = 1*<any character except an angle bracket or a line break>
stressed     = 1*<any character except a line break>
```

- A tag doesn’t cross a line break.
- Where text matches more than one rule, a span takes precedence over a delivery tag and a pause over a sound tag. Stressed words end at the first `^^` after them.
- Names are case-sensitive, and universal names and `pause` are lowercase. Spaces at either end of a name are ignored.
- An empty `<<>>` returns to the baseline, as `<<neutral>>` does. An empty `[[]]` is left out.
- A span can hold stressed words, but not another span or tag. Stressed words can’t hold a tag.
- RCS 0.1 has no escape. Text that matches a tag is read as one. An unpaired `^^`, or a `<<` or `[[` left open at the end of a response, is removed. Any other `<<` or `[[` that doesn’t start a tag is text.\
\
### [Navigate to header: Producer Requirements](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#producer-requirements-2) Producer Requirements\
\
- A producer SHOULD write only the deliveries and sounds the consumer declared, by their universal names where one exists.\
- A producer SHOULD write a pause only within the consumer’s declared range, and stress only when the consumer declared emphasis.\
- A producer MUST NOT write a tag inside a span or inside stressed words.\
- A producer MUST write stress as `^^words^^`, not as a delivery.\
\
### [Navigate to header: Consumer Requirements](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#consumer-requirements-2) Consumer Requirements\
\
- A consumer MUST NOT speak a tag. It MUST leave a tag it can’t perform out of the speech.\
- A consumer MUST read a tag’s kind from its brackets, except that a universal name, or a name the consumer declared, keeps its kind in the other brackets: `[[warm]]` still sets a delivery, and `<<laugh>>` is still a sound.\
- A consumer MUST remove an unfinished tag at the end of a response, or one cut off by an interruption, without speaking it.\
- A consumer MUST perform each delivery and sound it declared when it’s written by its universal name, as well as by the consumer’s own name.\
\
The agent SHOULD keep a reply the LLM wrote with tags in the conversation’s context as written, so later turns see how it was said.\
\
### [Navigate to header: Universal Names](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#universal-names) Universal Names\
\
Deliveries and sounds are named by their universal names, the same whatever the TTS model. A consumer translates each into its own name for it, such as a TTS model that performs `warm` as `warmly`.\
\
- **One spelling per word**: an adjective for a delivery, such as `nervous`, and a base word for a sound, such as `laugh`.\
- **Different words stay distinct**, so `content` and `happy` are both names.\
- **Only sounds a voice makes** have names. Sound effects, such as applause, have none.\
- **Any other name** passes through as written, for a consumer that takes free text, such as an accent.\
\
Two names are reserved: `neutral`, the voice’s baseline, and `emphasis`, the delivery reported for stressed words.\
\

### [Navigate to header: Reporting Delivery](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#reporting-delivery) Reporting Delivery\
\
A consumer that reports what it performed, such as to a client app, reports the delivery of each word as a list of universal names: the delivery in effect, a span’s delivery added to it, and `emphasis` for a stressed word. `<<warm>> it ^^did^^ ship` reports `did` as `["warm", "emphasis"]`. An empty list is the voice’s baseline. Each sound and pause is reported on its own, where it is performed.\
\
### [Navigate to header: Declaring Expression](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#declaring-expression) Declaring Expression\
\
A TTS model declares what it performs before the conversation starts, so the producer is offered only those tags:\
\
| Field | Meaning |\
| --- | --- |\
| Deliveries | The deliveries it performs, by its own names |\
| Sounds | The sounds it performs, by its own names |\
| Free text | Whether it also takes deliveries, or sounds, described in a few words, declared for each kind on its own |\
| Universal names | Its own name for each universal name, where they differ |\
| Pauses | The shortest and longest pause it makes, or none |\
| Emphasis | Whether it stresses words |\
| Where delivery changes | Anywhere in a response, or only between sentences. A model that changes it only between sentences speaks a span’s whole sentence in the span’s delivery |\
\

\
| Version | Changes |\
| --- | --- |\
| 0.1 | First version: perception and expression. |\
\
In 0.1, declarations don’t carry a version.\
\
## [Navigate to header: Implementations](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#implementations) Implementations\
\
- **Pipecat** 1.15.0 and later implement RCS 0.1 in [expressive conversation](https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/features/expressive-conversation).\
- **Pipecat clients** receive reported delivery, sounds, pauses and perception readings over [RTVI](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/rtvi-standard) 2.3.0 and later. RCS doesn’t define how context reaches client apps.\
\
## [Navigate to header: Roadmap](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#roadmap) Roadmap\
\
Context types under consideration for later versions:\
\
- **Diarization**: who is speaking, for conversations with more than one person.\
- **Intent**: when someone means to speak, and whether what they said needs a response.\
\
## [Navigate to header: Contributing](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/standards/real-time-context-standard\#contributing) Contributing\
\
RCS is an open standard, for any framework or model to produce and consume. To propose a change or a new context type, open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/pipecat-ai/pipecat/issues).\

I'm assuming you mean Deepgram's **Real-Time Context Standard (RCS)**, not RCS phone messaging. It's a different kind of thing from Flux. Flux is a set of models; RCS is an agreed text format for passing extra information between the parts of a voice app. Deepgram and the Pipecat team announced it on October 29, 2026. It's an early draft (version 0.1) and may change in ways that break existing code.

## What it solves

A voice app is a chain: speech-to-text, then a language model, then text-to-speech. Only the words get passed along. How the person sounded is lost, and so is how the reply should sound. RCS adds that back, written right into the text:

- **How the user sounded.** A short note goes in front of what they said, for example `([tone frustrated=0.86]) Where's my order?`. The language model can then react to the tone, not just the words.
- **How the reply should sound.** The language model, or a helper model, adds small tags that the voice model performs:
  - `<<warm>>` or `<<whisper>>` changes how the next words are said.
  - `^^did^^` stresses a word.
  - `[[laugh]]` adds a sound.
  - `[[pause 600]]` adds a 600 ms pause.

## How it could help OnceUpon

**The speaking side is the exciting part for a storybook.** Gemini could write the tags itself, for example `<<whisper>> Shh, the hare is sleeping... [[pause 800]]` or `Harry Hare [[laugh]] laughed, "You'll never catch me!"`. That's real acting, which is what bedtime stories need.

The catch is that the voice model has to understand the tags. Deepgram's demo used ElevenLabs and Cartesia voices. I haven't found confirmation that Aura-2 or Flux TTS read RCS tags yet. Without that, they'd either read them aloud or we'd have to strip them out.

**The listening side matters less for a kids' storybook.** Reading the child's emotion needs an extra model. The demo uses a separate Pipecat tool called Tone; Flux doesn't produce these readings on its own. Analyzing a child's emotions from their voice also raises privacy concerns, so I'd be careful with it.

## What adopting it involves

RCS is built around Pipecat, a Python framework that runs the whole voice chain on a server. OnceUpon runs its chain in the browser with Next.js. That leaves two paths:
- **Use only the tag format.** Have Gemini write the tags, and pass them to a voice model that understands them. This is a small change, but only if our voice model supports tags.
- **Move to Pipecat.** We'd get the full system, but it means rebuilding the app's voice pipeline. That's too big for the benefit right now.

## My recommendation

Not yet. It's an early draft, and the main win (expressive storytelling) depends on a voice model that reads the tags. I'd stick with the earlier order:
1. Switch listening to Flux STT.
2. Compare Flux TTS voices with Aura-2.
3. While doing that, check whether Flux TTS supports RCS tags. If it does, having Gemini write `<<whisper>>` and `[[laugh]]` would be a cheap, fun upgrade.

If you meant RCS messaging, the richer successor to texting, it doesn't really fit a voice storybook app. Say so if that's what you were after and I'll look into it.

# Turn-based audio (Flux STT)

GET /v2/listen

Real-time conversational speech recognition with contextual turn detection
for natural voice conversations


Reference: https://developers.deepgram.com/reference/speech-to-text/listen-flux

## AsyncAPI Specification

asyncapi: 2.6.0

    Real-time conversational speech recognition with contextual turn detection
    for natural voice conversations
channels:
  /v2/listen:
    description: |
      Real-time conversational speech recognition with contextual turn detection
      for natural voice conversations
    bindings:
      ws:
        query:
          type: object
          properties:
            model:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2Model'

            eot_threshold:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2EotThreshold'
              default: '0.7'
            eot_timeout_ms:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2EotTimeoutMs'
              default: '5000'
            keyterm:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2Keyterm'
            language_hint:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2LanguageHint'

              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2ProfanityFilter'

            numerals:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2Numerals'
              default: 'false'
            redact:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2Redact'

              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2RedactUsage'
              default: 'false'
            mip_opt_out:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2MipOptOut'
            tag:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2Tag'
        headers:
          type: object
          properties:
            Authorization:
              type: string
    publish:
      operationId: subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-publish
      summary: Server messages
      message:
        oneOf:
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-server-0-ListenV2Connected
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-server-1-ListenV2TurnInfo
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-server-2-ListenV2ConfigureSuccess
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-server-3-ListenV2ConfigureFailure
          - $ref: >-

          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-0-ListenV2Media
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-1-ListenV2CloseStream
          - $ref: >-
              #/components/messages/subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-2-ListenV2ForceEndTurn
          - $ref: >-

    subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-1-ListenV2CloseStream:
      name: ListenV2CloseStream
      title: ListenV2CloseStream
      description: Control messages for managing the Speech to Text WebSocket connection
      payload:
        $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2_ListenV2CloseStream'
    subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-2-ListenV2ForceEndTurn:
      name: ListenV2ForceEndTurn
      title: ListenV2ForceEndTurn
      description: >-
        Force the current turn to end immediately. Flux ends the turn on the

      payload:
        $ref: '#/components/schemas/ListenV2_ListenV2ForceEndTurn'
    subpackage_listen/v2.listen.v2-client-3-ListenV2Configure:

      description: Send a Configure message to update Flux settings

  schemas:
    ListenV2Model:
      type: string
      enum:
        - flux-general-en
        - flux-general-multi
      description: Defines the AI model used to process submitted audio.
      title: ListenV2Model
    ListenV2Encoding:
      type: string
      enum:
        - linear16
        - linear32
        - mulaw
        - alaw
        - opus
        - ogg-opus
      description: >-
        Encoding of the audio stream. Required if sending non-containerized/raw
        audio. If sending containerized audio, this parameter should be omitted.
      title: ListenV2Encoding
    ListenV2SampleRate:
      description: Any type
      title: ListenV2SampleRate
    ListenV2EagerEotThreshold:
      description: Any type
      title: ListenV2EagerEotThreshold
    ListenV2EotThreshold:
      description: Any type
      title: ListenV2EotThreshold
    ListenV2EotTimeoutMs:
      description: Any type
      title: ListenV2EotTimeoutMs
    ListenV2Keyterm:
      oneOf:
        - type: string
        - type: array
          items:
            type: string
      description: >
        Keyterm prompting improves recognition of specialized terminology.


        `keyterm` accepts plain terms only. Unlike the legacy `keywords`
        feature,

        it does not support weights or intensifiers. Appending one

        (for example, `keyterm=term:0.15`) is not rejected—the weight is

        silently ignored and the entire value is treated as a literal keyterm.


        To boost multiple separate keyterms, repeat the `keyterm` parameter

        (for example, `keyterm=term1&keyterm=term2`). To boost one multi-word

        phrase as a single keyterm, join the words with `%20` or `+`

        (for example, `keyterm=customer%20service`). Do not separate keyterms

        with commas, semicolons, or line breaks.
      title: ListenV2Keyterm
    ListenV2LanguageHint:
      oneOf:
        - type: string
        - type: array
          items:
            type: string
      description: |
        Language hints constrain and prioritize language detection for the
        flux-general-multi model. Pass multiple language_hint query parameters
        to specify multiple language codes. Empty values are rejected.
        Only valid when model is flux-general-multi.
      title: ListenV2LanguageHint
    ListenV2ProfanityFilter:
      type: string
      enum:
        - 'true'
        - 'false'
      default: 'false'
      description: >-
        Profanity Filter looks for recognized profanity and converts it to the
        nearest recognized non-profane word or removes it from the transcript
        completely.
      title: ListenV2ProfanityFilter
    ListenV2Numerals:
      type: string
      enum:
        - 'true'
        - 'false'
      default: 'false'
      description: Numerals converts numbers from written format to numerical format
      title: ListenV2Numerals
    ListenV2Redact:
      type: string
      enum:
        - numbers
        - aggressive_numbers
      description: >-
        Redaction removes sensitive information from your transcripts. On Flux,
        only `numbers` and `aggressive_numbers` are supported.
      title: ListenV2Redact

      description: >-
        Replaces keyterms and other user-supplied text with `[REDACTED]` in this
        connection's usage records, including keyterms sent in later Configure
        messages. Does not affect transcription, the response, or `tag`.
        Independent of `mip_opt_out`.
        https://developers.deepgram.com/docs/redact-usage
      title: ListenV2RedactUsage

      type: string
      enum:
        - Update
        - StartOfTurn
        - EagerEndOfTurn

        - **Update** - Additional audio has been transcribed, but the turn state

# Understanding the Flux STT state machine

Emitted events adhere to the below state machine for managing turns:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR

  [*] --> Initial
  Initial --> TurnOngoing : StartOfTurn
  TurnOngoing --> AwaitingEnd : EagerEndOfTurn
  AwaitingEnd --> TurnOngoing : TurnResumed
  AwaitingEnd --> Initial : EndOfTurn
  TurnOngoing --> Initial : ForceEndTurn
  AwaitingEnd --> Initial : ForceEndTurn

  state Initial {
    [*] --> Ready
  }

  state TurnOngoing {
    [*] --> Speaking
  }

  state AwaitingEnd {
    [*] --> Processing
  }
```

1. `Update` messages are sent for approximately every 0.25 seconds of transcribed audio, regardless of transcript updates, unless a state change has occurred.
2. An `EagerEndOfTurn` message always contains a nonempty transcript.
3. A `TurnResumed` message can only follow a preceding `EagerEndOfTurn` message.
4. The `EndOfTurn` transcript will always match the immediately preceding `EagerEndOfTurn` transcript. If the transcript changes after an `EagerEndOfTurn`, a `TurnResumed` event will occur first.
5. The `turn_index` increments immediately following an `EndOfTurn` message.
6. When using `flux-general-multi`, all `TurnInfo` events include `languages` (detected languages sorted by word count) and `languages_hinted` (active language hints). See [Language Prompting](/docs/flux/language-prompting).
7. Every `EndOfTurn` event includes a `trigger` field — `model` (native detection), `manual` ([`ForceEndTurn`](/docs/flux/force-end-turn)), or `timeout` (`eot_timeout_ms`) — indicating what ended the turn.
8. You can end the current turn at any time by sending a [`ForceEndTurn`](/docs/flux/force-end-turn) message. Deepgram Flux STT emits an `EndOfTurn` with `trigger: "manual"` from any in-turn state.

> **Info**
>
> **Configuring Event Behavior**: The `EagerEndOfTurn` and `TurnResumed` events are only triggered when you set the `eager_eot_threshold` parameter. The `EndOfTurn` event behavior is controlled by `eot_threshold` and `eot_timeout_ms` parameters. See the [End-of-Turn Configuration](/docs/flux/configuration) for details on tuning these thresholds for your use case.

> **Info**
>
> **Barge-in and audio quality**: Flux STT's `StartOfTurn` event is the recommended way to trigger barge-in — it's more reliable than an external VAD because every `StartOfTurn` is guaranteed to contain a non-empty transcript. For guidance on echo cancellation, noise suppression, and other audio preprocessing that affects turn detection, see [Audio preprocessing & barge-in](/guides/deep-dives/audio-preprocessing-barge-in).

## Turn lifecycle example

Here's how Flux STT processes a customer calling support saying "Hi I need to cancel my subscription please."

Notice how confidence builds up and how the `EagerEndOfTurn` event fires before the final `EndOfTurn`. With `EagerEndOfTurn`, your voice agent can begin preparing a response before the user has fully finished speaking. This allows you to send a synchronous request with early context, creating the effect of a faster, more natural reply.

# Getting started with Flux TTS batch (REST)

The batch (REST) transport synthesizes a complete block of text and returns the full audio in one response. Use it to pre-generate fixed audio — IVR prompts, notifications, audiobook lines — where the whole text is known up front and you don't need incremental playback or interruption. For live, interruptible conversations, use the [real-time WebSocket](/docs/flux-tts/quickstart) instead (see [Batch vs Streaming](/docs/flux-tts/batch-vs-streaming)).

Batch is stateless request/response: simple retries, high fan-out, no connection lifecycle to manage. It serves the same Deepgram Flux TTS voices as the streaming transport.

## Make a request

```bash
curl "https://api.deepgram.com/v2/speak?model=flux-haley-en" \
  -H "Authorization: Token REDACTED" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "text": "Your appointment is confirmed for 3pm tomorrow." }' \
  --output audio.mp3
```

The response body is the synthesized audio in the requested encoding. Per-request telemetry is returned as response headers, mirroring Deepgram Aura's REST conventions — character counts and the generic `dg-warnings` header.

## Query parameters

| Parameter         | Default              | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `model`           | —                    | **Required.** A `flux-{voice}-{language}` model (e.g. `flux-haley-en`).                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `encoding`        | `mp3`                | `mp3`, `opus`, `flac`, `aac` (containerized/compressed), or raw `linear16` / `mulaw` / `alaw`.                                                                                                                                                 |
| `bit_rate`        | per-encoding default | Bit rate for compressed encodings. For `mp3`: `8000`, `16000`, `24000`, `32000`, `40000`, `48000`.                                                                                                                                             |
| `container`       | per-encoding default | Output container where applicable (e.g. `wav` for `linear16`, `ogg` for `opus`).                                                                                                                                                               |
| `sample_rate`     | model native         | Sample rate; supported values depend on `encoding`. `linear16`: `8000`, `16000`, `24000`, `32000`, `44100`, `48000`. `mulaw` / `alaw`: `8000`, `16000`. `flac`: `8000`, `16000`, `22050`, `32000`, `48000`. Not applicable to `mp3` or `opus`. |
| `speed`           | `1.0`                | Speech-rate multiplier — `0.5` to `1.5` in `0.05` increments. Not supported by every model or language; unsupported combinations return `SPEED_NOT_SUPPORTED`.                                                                                 |
| `expressivity`    | `0`                  | **Beta.** Delivery register, `-2` (calm) to `2` (animated). See [Expressivity](/docs/tts-expressivity).                                                                                                                                        |
| `callback`        | —                    | URL to receive the result asynchronously, instead of on the response body.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `callback_method` | `POST`               | HTTP method for the callback request (`POST` or `PUT`).                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `priority`        | —                    | Prioritization for asynchronous (callback) requests. Only value: `Low`.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `tag`             | —                    | Label requests for usage reporting. Repeatable.                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `mip_opt_out`     | `false`              | Opt out of the Model Improvement Program.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

> **Info**
>
> Conversational constructs (`Flush`, `Interrupt`, `speech_id`, lifecycle events) do not apply to batch. `model`, `speed`, `expressivity`, and the media-output settings behave the same as on the [streaming surface](/docs/flux-tts/quickstart), so the contract doesn't fragment across transports. The one difference is inline pause: it's supported on batch only. See [Speed, pause, pronunciation](/docs/tts-voice-controls#combining-controls).

## When to use batch vs streaming

See [Batch vs streaming: which should I use?](/docs/flux-tts/batch-vs-streaming) for the decision guide.

# Migrating from /v1/speak to Flux TTS

Deepgram Flux TTS ships on a new endpoint, `/v2/speak`. The `/v1/speak` endpoint stays available and unchanged, and all Deepgram Aura model strings continue to work on it — there's no aliasing, redirect, or deprecation. You migrate when you're ready to build on the streaming-first surface.

## Which should you use?

**Use Flux TTS** for new voice-agent work: streaming LLM output, barge-in, and multi-turn conversations where tone should carry across turns.

**Stay on Aura** if you're using Aura voices. Aura voices are served only on `/v1/speak`; Flux TTS voices only on `/v2/speak` (where a `flux-*` model is required).

## What changes

| Dimension          | `/v1/speak`                              | `/v2/speak` (Flux TTS)                                                                                                 |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mental model       | Text buffer → audio stream               | Streaming-first, turn-based conversation                                                                               |
| Text input         | `Speak` messages into a global buffer    | `Speak` messages; server tracks the active turn and assigns `speech_id` (informational)                                |
| Flushing           | Manual `Flush` + flush toggles           | `Flush` signals no more text is coming for the turn; once its synthesis completes, you get the turn's `SpeechMetadata` |
| Interruption       | `Clear` discards the buffer, no feedback | `Interrupt` with spoken-text feedback (`text_spoken` / `text_remaining`)                                               |
| Context reset      | None (reconnect the WebSocket)           | Not needed — prosody carries across turns automatically (no API surface)                                               |
| Turn metadata      | None                                     | You mark end-of-turn with `Flush` and get per-turn `SpeechMetadata` (billing, timing) back                             |
| Dynamic config     | None (fixed at connection)               | Mid-stream `Configure` for `speed`                                                                                     |
| Cross-turn context | None                                     | Model state persists across turns                                                                                      |

## Migration steps

1. **Change the endpoint.** Point your WebSocket at `/v2/speak` (was `/v1/speak`). The Python (`deepgram-sdk`) and JavaScript (`@deepgram/sdk`) SDKs expose a `speak.v2` client — see [Getting Started](/docs/flux-tts/quickstart) and the [template apps](/docs/flux-tts/template-apps) — or integrate against the WebSocket directly.
2. **Keep your `Speak` messages.** The `Speak` shape is unchanged. Do **not** specify `speech_id` — the server assigns it and returns it for debuggability.
3. **Require a `model`.** `model` is required on every `/v2/speak` connection. Use a Flux TTS voice string (e.g. `flux-haley-en`); Aura voices are served by `/v1/speak`, not `/v2/speak`.
4. **Replace `Clear` with `Interrupt`.** End each turn with `Flush`; on barge-in, send `Interrupt` and use the returned `text_spoken` / `text_remaining` to reconcile your LLM context — see [Interruption handling](/docs/flux-tts/interrupt-handling).
5. **Treat `Flush` as end-of-turn, and read `SpeechMetadata`.** `Flush` marks the end of a turn (there's no separate `Finalize`). The turn's `SpeechMetadata` reports billing and timing — use it as your end-of-turn signal (not `Flushed`), and drop any client-side character-count or audio-duration tracking.
6. **Drop the flush toggles.** The v1 `flush_send`-style toggles don't exist on v2 — audio starts streaming for a turn on its own, and you `Flush` only to mark the end of the turn.
7. **Drop reconnect-to-reset logic.** Prosody carries across turns automatically; there's no reset step to port.
8. **Insert whitespace between distinct LLM responses.** The server doesn't add whitespace between `Speak` messages — see [Text handling](/docs/flux-tts/client-messages#text-handling).

## Message mapping

The `/v2/speak` column mixes messages you send (`Speak`, `Flush`, `Close`) with messages the server sends back (`Connected`, `Flushed`, `SpeechMetadata`, `SessionMetadata`). See [Client messages](/docs/flux-tts/client-messages) and [Server messages](/docs/flux-tts/server-messages) for the full split.

| `/v1/speak`            | `/v2/speak`                                    |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `Speak`                | `Speak` (unchanged)                            |
| `Flush` (buffer flush) | `Flush` (ends the turn)                        |
| `Clear`                | `Interrupt`                                    |
| `Finalize`             | folded into `Flush`                            |
| `Metadata` (on open)   | `Connected`                                    |
| `Flushed` / `Cleared`  | `Flushed`, `SpeechMetadata`, `SessionMetadata` |
| `Close`                | `Close` (+ final `SessionMetadata`)            |

## Behaviors carried forward

* The **`Speak`** message shape is unchanged from v1.
* **1-hour max session duration** carries over from v1. New on v2: a **60s inactivity timeout** (`NET-0004`) — send a WebSocket Ping (or Pong) to keep long-idle sessions alive.

Markup handling carries its own warning codes. Inline pronunciation (Early Access) works on both transports and inline pause on batch only, with stricter combination rules than Aura-2 (see [Speed, pause, pronunciation](/docs/tts-voice-controls#combining-controls)) — see [Markup handling](/docs/flux-tts/client-messages#markup-handling) and the [warning codes](/docs/flux-tts/server-messages#warning-codes).

## Related resources

\# Flux TTS Voices & Languages

Deepgram Flux TTS voices use the model string format \`flux-{voice}-{language}\` (e.g. \`flux-haley-en\`). The same voice catalog is served on both \`/v2/speak\` transports — the \[streaming WebSocket\](/docs/flux-tts/quickstart) and \[batch REST\](/docs/flux-tts/batch). Every voice in every language is also available in the \[Voice Agent API\](/docs/voice-agent-tts-models#flux-tts).

\## Selecting a voice

Pass the model string on connection:

\`\`\`
wss://api.deepgram.com/v2/speak?model=flux-haley-en
\`\`\`

Every voice handles general conversational synthesis. Use the tables below to shortlist, then hear the voices live at \[talk.deepgram.com\](https://talk.deepgram.com) before you build.

\## Languages

Flux TTS voices speak English — with accents spanning American, British, Irish, Australian, Indian, Singaporean, and Filipino English — and 41 other languages:

Bengali (\`bn\`), Bulgarian (\`bg\`), Catalan (\`ca\`), Chinese (\`zh\`), Croatian (\`hr\`), Czech (\`cs\`), Danish (\`da\`), Dutch (\`nl\`), Estonian (\`et\`), Finnish (\`fi\`), French (\`fr\`), German (\`de\`), Greek (\`el\`), Gujarati (\`gu\`), Hindi (\`hi\`), Hungarian (\`hu\`), Indonesian (\`id\`), Italian (\`it\`), Japanese (\`ja\`), Kannada (\`kn\`), Korean (\`ko\`), Latvian (\`lv\`), Lithuanian (\`lt\`), Malay (\`ms\`), Marathi (\`mr\`), Norwegian (\`no\`), Polish (\`pl\`), Portuguese (\`pt\`), Romanian (\`ro\`), Russian (\`ru\`), Slovak (\`sk\`), Slovenian (\`sl\`), Spanish (\`es\`), Swedish (\`sv\`), Tagalog (\`tl\`), Tamil (\`ta\`), Telugu (\`te\`), Turkish (\`tr\`), Ukrainian (\`uk\`), Urdu (\`ur\`), Vietnamese (\`vi\`).

Languages marked Early Access don't have text normalization yet: numbers, dates, and abbreviations are read as written, so write them out in words. Text normalization is available for English, German, Dutch, French, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish.

The voices in these 41 languages are available on \`api.deepgram.com\`, \`api.eu.deepgram.com\`, and \`api.in.deepgram.com\`; they aren't yet available on the Australia endpoint (\`api.au.deepgram.com\`).

\# Flux TTS Voices & Languages

Deepgram Flux TTS voices use the model string format \`flux-{voice}-{language}\` (e.g. \`flux-haley-en\`). The same voice catalog is served on both \`/v2/speak\` transports — the \[streaming WebSocket\](/docs/flux-tts/quickstart) and \[batch REST\](/docs/flux-tts/batch). Every voice in every language is also available in the \[Voice Agent API\](/docs/voice-agent-tts-models#flux-tts).

\## Selecting a voice

Pass the model string on connection:

\`\`\`
wss://api.deepgram.com/v2/speak?model=flux-haley-en
\`\`\`

Every voice handles general conversational synthesis. Use the tables below to shortlist, then hear the voices live at \[talk.deepgram.com\](https://talk.deepgram.com) before you build.

\## Languages

Flux TTS voices speak English — with accents spanning American, British, Irish, Australian, Indian, Singaporean, and Filipino English — and 41 other languages:

Bengali (\`bn\`), Bulgarian (\`bg\`), Catalan (\`ca\`), Chinese (\`zh\`), Croatian (\`hr\`), Czech (\`cs\`), Danish (\`da\`), Dutch (\`nl\`), Estonian (\`et\`), Finnish (\`fi\`), French (\`fr\`), German (\`de\`), Greek (\`el\`), Gujarati (\`gu\`), Hindi (\`hi\`), Hungarian (\`hu\`), Indonesian (\`id\`), Italian (\`it\`), Japanese (\`ja\`), Kannada (\`kn\`), Korean (\`ko\`), Latvian (\`lv\`), Lithuanian (\`lt\`), Malay (\`ms\`), Marathi (\`mr\`), Norwegian (\`no\`), Polish (\`pl\`), Portuguese (\`pt\`), Romanian (\`ro\`), Russian (\`ru\`), Slovak (\`sk\`), Slovenian (\`sl\`), Spanish (\`es\`), Swedish (\`sv\`), Tagalog (\`tl\`), Tamil (\`ta\`), Telugu (\`te\`), Turkish (\`tr\`), Ukrainian (\`uk\`), Urdu (\`ur\`), Vietnamese (\`vi\`).

Languages marked Early Access don't have text normalization yet: numbers, dates, and abbreviations are read as written, so write them out in words. Text normalization is available for English, German, Dutch, French, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish.

The voices in these 41 languages are available on \`api.deepgram.com\`, \`api.eu.deepgram.com\`, and \`api.in.deepgram.com\`; they aren't yet available on the Australia endpoint (\`api.au.deepgram.com\`).
